issues.issue: This legend flatly prohibits any reproduction or distribution of the Memorandum without the Manager's prior written consent, while the CONFIDENTIAL/TRADE SECRET legend (c011) expressly permits the recipient to distribute it to his own financial and legal advisors. A court would have to decide which of the two permission regimes governs a disclosure to advisors.

The legend requires investors to rely solely on their own examination of the Notes and the offering, whereas the Conflicts of Interest sections (c038, c050) state that Noteholders 'must rely on the good faith and integrity of the Manager.' The two allocations of reliance cannot easily be given effect together in a misrepresentation dispute.

This legend states categorically that the Company 'will not be registered as an investment company,' while the Risk Factor 'Company Not Registered' (c206) admits there is no assurance the Company will not become subject to the Investment Company Act. Whether the legend is a promise or merely a present expectation is left open.

The legend permits transfer 'except as provided in the Note Purchase Agreement referred to herein,' but the Note Purchase Agreement (§7) forbids all transfers absent the Company's consent while the Memorandum's 'Transfers of Notes' term (c124) carves out family trusts, wholly-owned affiliates and operation of law. The permitted-transfer set therefore differs depending on which document is read.

The Company's undertaking to furnish additional information is bounded only by what it can obtain 'without unreasonable effort or expense,' a standard the Memorandum nowhere defines or measures. The scope of the disclosure obligation therefore has no ascertainable boundary.

The sentence is joined by a comma splice ('THE COMPANY BELIEVES THAT SUCH INFORMATION IS ACCURATE ..., THE COMPANY CANNOT GUARANTEE THE ACCURACY'), so it reads as both an affirmation and a disclaimer of the same third-party data. The punctuation makes it unclear whether any representation of accuracy is being made at all.

The Manager and its affiliates reserve the right to modify any term of the offering and the Offering Documents before the final closing, which cannot be squared with 'Amendments, Waivers of Noteholder Agreements' (c131) requiring the written approval of a Majority in Interest of Noteholders for any modification of the Note Purchase Agreement, Notes or Security Agreement. A court would have to decide which controls for a Noteholder whose Note is issued at an earlier closing.

'We may terminate this offering at any time before a closing' does not say whether 'a closing' means the Initial Closing or any of the successive closings contemplated by the Closing term (c109), so the termination right's expiry date is indeterminate. The singular article gives the sentence two reasonable readings.

This legend allows the recipient to consult and give copies to his own financial and legal advisors, whereas the opening confidentiality legend (c001) prohibits reproduction or distribution 'in whole or in part' without the Manager's prior written consent. The two confidentiality undertakings impose inconsistent duties on the same recipient.

The Executive Summary states without qualification that 'The Notes will be secured by the assets of the Company,' but the Use of capital paragraph (c019) and the Company Borrowings term (c125) permit borrowings secured by liens senior to the lien securing the Notes. Whether investors were promised a first-priority security interest is left to be construed from the two passages together.

The offer of 'superior returns with a conservative risk profile' and a target of 'approximately 8.00% or more per year' conflicts with the Risk Factors' statement that the purchase of Notes involves a high degree of risk and that investors must be able to lose their entire investment (c169, c207). A court could be asked whether the summary's characterization is a term of the bargain or mere puffery displaced by the risk section.

The stated purpose confines Portfolio Loans to commercial real estate and related purposes 'throughout the United States,' but the Geographic Area of Lending Activity provision (c059) permits up to 20% of Company capital to be lent on non-U.S. properties and the General Standards (c056) permit residential construction loans. The scope of permitted lending differs depending on which provision governs.

This paragraph says the Manager only 'expects to hire' Bar-K, Inc. as Servicer, whereas the Bar-K, Inc., the Servicer section (c030) states that the Manager 'has selected' Bar-K and the Servicer term (c084) makes Bar-K the initial Servicer. Whether the engagement of the affiliate Servicer was already fixed is left in doubt.

The Summary says closings are expected on the first day of each calendar month 'through May 1, 2009,' while the Closing term (c109) sets the final closing at the last day of the sixth full quarter after the Initial Closing (estimated June 30, 2009) and the Note Purchase Agreement (§2.1) contemplates quarterly closings. The end of the subscription period and the closing frequency cannot be reconciled across the three statements.

The Summary promises 'a minimum average rate of eight percent (8%) annualized,' whereas the Floating Rate term (c089) and Note Purchase Agreement §1.3 impose a floor of 8% for each calendar year rather than an average. A rate averaging 8% but falling below 8% in some quarters would satisfy one provision and breach the other.

This paragraph states that a Noteholder may request prepayment after holding the Note one year, omitting the further conditions imposed by the Return of Investment term (c103) and Note Purchase Agreement §1.4(a)(ii) — sixty days' notice and a quarter-end effective date. Which set of conditions governs a prepayment request must be construed.

The statement that Noteholders 'will be secured creditors of the Company' sits against the Use of capital paragraph (c019) and Failure of Security risk factor (c200), which permit the Noteholders' security interest to be subordinated to Company Borrowings and give no assurance of perfection. The quality of the creditor status conferred is only ascertainable by reading those provisions together.

This paragraph permits borrowings secured by liens on Company assets 'senior to the lien securing the Notes,' which cannot be squared with the Executive Summary's unqualified statement that the Notes will be secured by the assets of the Company (c012) and that Noteholders are secured creditors (c018). A court would have to decide whether the senior-lien authority qualifies the security promise.

The covenant that the Company 'will not operate in the sub-prime mortgage market and will not source loans for the purpose of resale' cannot be squared with Credit Evaluations (c063), which expressly permits loans to borrowers in default on other obligations or without qualifying income, and with Sale of Loans Generally (c078), which permits occasional resale. What counts as sub-prime lending or sourcing for resale would have to be construed against those provisions.

The assertion that 'no investor has experienced a loss of investment principal through investment vehicles sponsored by the Principals' is an unqualified historical representation that the projections disclaimer (c026) purports to reduce to illustration only. Whether the track-record statement survives that disclaimer as a representation is open.

The description of R.E. Loans' $750 million portfolio and 8.5% average investor returns says nothing of R.E. Loans' secured credit facility, the Loan and Security Agreement with Wells Fargo Foothill dated July 17, 2007 filed in this case, under which its notes receivable were pledged. Read with that instrument, the portrayal of the affiliate whose loans the Company expects to buy (c055) is materially incomplete.

The claim that Bar-K 'has a 100% collection record with respect to loans it administers' sits against the Sale of Defaulted Loans provisions (c053, c077) and the tax discussion (c151), which describe the affiliates' practice of buying defaulting loans out of the fund. Whether a collection record achieved by affiliate repurchase is what the sentence represents would have to be construed.

This disclaimer treats everything said about prior results as 'historical only' and 'for illustration purposes,' which cannot readily be squared with the specific affirmative claims in Investor Opportunities (c022) and Bar-K servicing (c025) that no investor has lost principal and that Bar-K has a 100% collection record. A court would have to decide whether the disclaimer negates those representations.

This section states that the four members of B-4 Partners LLC are Walter Ng, Bruce Horwitz, Barney Ng and Kelly Ng, while Other Funds or Businesses (c047) describes B-4 Partners LLC as 'owned and managed by Walter Ng and Dr. Bruce Horwitz.' The ownership of the affiliate that manages R.E. Loans is stated two different ways.

The sentence describes Bar-K as 'a real estate broker licensed by the California Department of Corporations,' mismatching the licence to the licensing agency (real estate brokers are licensed by the Department of Real Estate; finance lenders by the Department of Corporations). The error clouds what licences the Servicer actually holds, a point the Lending Laws discussion (c165, c166) makes material.

'The Servicer will originate or arrange all loans acquired by the Company' cannot be squared with the Manager's right to retain other firms in lieu of the Servicer (c042) or with Purchase of Loans from Servicer (c072), which allows purchases from unrelated third parties. Whether the Servicer has an exclusive origination role is left in doubt.

The Manager's reserved right to terminate all or any portion of its business relationship with the Company 'at any time' conflicts with Restricted Actions (c126) and Note Purchase Agreement §6.2(e), which bar withdrawal of the sole manager without the approval of a Majority in Interest of Noteholders. The two provisions give opposite answers to whether the Manager may walk away unilaterally.

This paragraph makes the payee of Loan Services compensation turn on whether the Company or the Manager contracts with the Servicer, whereas Note Purchase Agreement §5.4 makes all such fees payable to the Manager (or its designee) in every case. Which document determines who is entitled to the Loan Servicing Fee must be resolved.

The paragraph opens by stating that under Delaware law a manager is accountable to the company's members as a fiduciary, then concludes that the Manager has no fiduciary obligation to the Company's members because it is itself the sole member. The passage both asserts and disclaims the same duty, leaving the Manager's actual duty to be construed.

This paragraph states the indemnity and exculpation standard as 'fraud, bad faith or willful misconduct,' while the Exculpation and Indemnification term (c132) and Note Purchase Agreement §5.5(c) state it as 'willful misconduct or gross negligence.' Grossly negligent conduct is indemnified under one formulation and not the other.

Requiring Noteholders to 'rely on the good faith and integrity of the Manager' is difficult to square with the same section's conclusion (c034) and Note Purchase Agreement §4.3 that the Manager owes the Noteholders no fiduciary or similar duty. Whether any enforceable good-faith obligation is created by this sentence is open.

The closing cross-reference is to '(See "Fiduciary Responsibility of the Managing Member.")', a section that does not exist in the Memorandum — the corresponding heading is 'No Fiduciary Responsibility of Manager to Noteholders' (c034), and 'Managing Member' is nowhere defined. The reader is pointed to a provision that cannot be located.

The brokerage, renewal and forbearance fees the Servicer may charge Portfolio Borrowers are described only as anticipated to be 'in the amount set forth herein' but 'may be higher or lower depending upon market conditions,' with no ceiling. The provision states a figure and then removes any boundary on it.

The Manager's right to retain other firms 'in lieu of the Servicer' conflicts with the statement that the Servicer 'will originate or arrange all loans acquired by the Company' (c031) and with the Servicer term (c084) naming Bar-K as Servicer. Whether Bar-K's role is exclusive or displaceable must be construed.

'Related Party Loans' is defined here as loans to persons affiliated with the Manager, Members or Servicer, but Note Purchase Agreement §5.7(e) defines the term by reference to 'Affiliate' and expressly excludes loans to Sponsored Investment Funds and Private Clients. The class of loans subject to the related-party limits differs between the two documents.

This limit is 20% of total Company assets 'at any time,' whereas the parallel Portfolio Loan Criteria provision (c071) tests the 20% only 'upon the closing of the Related Party Loan in question' and Note Purchase Agreement §5.7(e)(ii) measures 20% of the Loan Portfolio immediately after making the loan. A continuous covenant and a point-in-time test on different denominators cannot both be applied.

The condition requires Related Party Loans to be consistent with 'the lending standards and policies set forth above,' but no lending standards appear above this point in the Memorandum — they are set out later in Section IV (c056–c063). The referent of 'set forth above' cannot be identified.

This provision requires the Manager to purchase a defaulted Related Party Loan 'at par,' while Note Purchase Agreement §5.7(e)(iii) fixes the price at no less than outstanding principal plus accrued interest. The two formulas produce different prices where interest has accrued, and 'material event of default' is left undefined in both.

The Manager's allocation of loan opportunities between the Company and Other Sponsored Investment Funds is governed only by 'consideration of all relevant factors, including' an open list, which sets no standard a Noteholder could enforce. The catch-all swallows the enumerated factors of loan size, diversification, remaining term and uncommitted capital.

The direction that Noteholders 'must rely on the Manager to act in good faith' sits against the express disclaimer of any fiduciary or similar duty to Noteholders (c034 and Note Purchase Agreement §4.3). Whether this sentence creates an obligation or merely describes the investors' predicament is unresolved.

The Manager and Principals are to devote 'only so much time to the business of the Company as is reasonably required,' a measure with no stated benchmark and no minimum. The commitment cannot be tested against anything in the Memorandum.

The Manager's obligation on a defaulted loan is that its 'first priority will usually be' to obtain full recovery 'or so much thereof as can reasonably be obtained in light of current market conditions' — 'usually' and 'reasonably' leave the duty without any fixed content. It is unclear whether any enforceable obligation is created at all.

This provision sets an affiliate purchase price 'not less than' the independently appraised value, whereas Note Purchase Agreement §5.7(b)(ii) requires a price 'no higher than the independently appraised value of such property at the time of sale.' The two documents impose opposite constraints against the same appraisal figure.

'A purchase price ... which is not less than any of the following: (i) ... (ii) ... or (iii)' is ambiguous between a price at or above the highest of the three measures and a price at or above any one of them. The disjunctive 'any ... or' makes the pricing floor indeterminate.

This paragraph states that purchases from and co-investments with R.E. Loans will comply with 'lending criteria for such loans established by the Note Purchase Agreement,' but Note Purchase Agreement §5.3(e) permits the Company to buy and sell Portfolio Loans from Sponsored Investment Funds 'on such terms and conditions as the Manager, in its sole discretion, determines.' Whether any criteria in fact constrain these affiliate transactions must be construed.

The General Standards permit the Company to invest indirectly by acquiring an ownership interest in an entity holding a loan and to make loans 'collateralized by loans,' neither of which is a loan secured by a lien against real property as promised in the Executive Summary (c013). What a 'Portfolio Loan' may be is described inconsistently across the two provisions.

The loan-to-value table is introduced as 'a strict set of guidelines,' but the Loan-to-Value Ratios paragraph (c060) says the ratios 'generally will not exceed' those percentages and the exceptions paragraph (c061) disapplies them altogether for purchase-money and refinance loans. Whether the 70%/50% figures are binding limits or aspirations must be construed from the three provisions together.

The 20% cap on junior-lien loans is measured against 'the Company's entire Loan Portfolio,' a term the Memorandum never defines and which could mean aggregate principal, number of loans or committed capital. The cap therefore has no ascertainable denominator.

The 20% non-U.S. allowance is measured against 'total Company Capital,' whereas Note Purchase Agreement §6.1(g) measures the same 20% against 'the aggregate principal of all Portfolio Loans.' The two denominators yield different permitted amounts of foreign lending.

This provision says the ratios 'generally will not exceed' the stated percentages and permits the value to be fixed 'by either the Manager or an independent written appraisal,' which cannot be squared with the description of those percentages as 'a strict set of guidelines' (c057). A limit that the Manager may both value into compliance and generally observe is not a limit in the same sense.

The exception declares that purchase-money financing to persons affiliated with the Manager, Members or Servicer 'shall not constitute a Related Party Loan,' removing such financing from the 20% cap and default-repurchase duty in c044 and c046 and from the definition in Note Purchase Agreement §5.7(e). The two treatments of affiliate financing cannot both be given effect.

Company loans 'will generally have a term of between one (1) and six (6) years,' but every Note matures December 31, 2014 (c088) and the Company's term ends two years later (c123), so a six-year loan made during the subscription period would outlast the Notes it secures. The loan-term policy and the Note maturity cannot both be honoured.

This provision subordinates creditworthiness to loan-to-value and expressly permits loans to borrowers already in default or without qualifying income, which is difficult to square with the covenant that the Company 'will not operate in the sub-prime mortgage market' (c020) and with the promise of 'conservatively underwritten' loans. A court would have to decide which describes the Company's actual underwriting obligation.

The escrow condition requires 'satisfactory title insurance coverage' without saying to whom it must be satisfactory or by what standard, while the second sentence then lists the many risks title insurance does not cover. The condition's content is left undetermined.

The parenthetical directs the reader to 'VII. Risk Factors – Uninsured Losses,' but no subsection of that name exists in the Risk Factors section; the nearest is 'Inadequate Preservation of Collateral' (c186). The cross-reference points to a provision that is not in the instrument.

Item (c) is listed as one of the conditions the escrow agent must see satisfied before disbursing funds (c064), yet it states only that the Manager does not intend to arrange mortgage insurance — a disclosure, not a condition capable of being met. Its status within the escrow conditions is incoherent.

The requirement that 'Company investments in Loans will not be held in the name of the Manager or any other nominee' conflicts with the General Standards (c056), which permit the Company to hold a loan indirectly through an entity formed for the sole purpose of holding it. Whether such indirect holding is a prohibited nominee arrangement must be construed.

This provision tests the 20% Related Party Loan cap only 'upon the closing of the Related Party Loan in question,' whereas the Conflicts of Interest limitation (c044) makes the cap apply to aggregate Related Party Loans 'at any time.' A continuing covenant and a closing-date test give different answers whenever Company assets later shrink.

The price cap — 'generally' no more than the lower of par or fair market value — is immediately qualified by permission to pay a premium whenever the Manager believes the price 'is fair and reasonable and in the best interests of the Company.' The word 'generally' and the discretionary exception leave no ascertainable ceiling.

Loans bought from or sold to Sponsored Investment Funds must be 'priced at fair market value or better for the Company,' whereas Note Purchase Agreement §5.7(d) requires net sales proceeds equal to the greater of the unpaid balance or fair market value and §5.3(e) leaves such transactions to the Manager's sole discretion. The pricing constraint on affiliate loan transfers differs between the documents.

This provision subjects a transaction with a Noteholder to affiliated-transaction criteria only where the Noteholder is a related party or a Sponsored Investment Fund, while Note Purchase Agreement §5.8 requires every Noteholder loan transaction to be no less advantageous to the Company than an arm's-length transaction. The protection afforded on ordinary Noteholder transactions differs between the two.

The diversification limit runs 'after the second year of the Company's term' and is measured against '20% of the capital of the Company,' but the Memorandum never fixes when the Company's term begins nor defines its 'capital.' Neither the trigger date nor the denominator can be determined from the instrument.

The contingency reserve is left entirely to the Manager — whether to have one, in what amount, and funded 'from any source, including capital raised from the sale of Notes' — with no stated limit. There is no benchmark by which any reserve decision could be measured.

This provision permits sales of non-performing Portfolio Loans and foreclosed property to the Servicer or affiliates for restructuring or repositioning without any pricing constraint, whereas the affiliate-sale pricing standards (c054) and Note Purchase Agreement §5.7(b)–(d) impose minimum prices on exactly such sales. Whether the pricing floors apply to these sales must be construed.

This paragraph states only that the Company 'does not presently intend' to invest for resale and may 'occasionally sell mortgage loans,' whereas Private Mortgage Lending (c020) states flatly that the Company 'will not source loans for the purpose of resale.' A covenant and a present intention are being made to do the same work.

The leveraging provision lets the Company borrow from third-party lenders to fund loans without saying that such borrowings may prime the Noteholders' security, a consequence stated only in c019, c125 and c200. Read alone this provision misdescribes the Noteholders' position in the capital structure.

Subscriptions are said to be accepted 'in the discretion of the Managing Member,' a term never defined in the Memorandum, which elsewhere vests acceptance in the Manager (c087, c213) or the Company (c015). Who has power to accept a subscription cannot be determined from the words used.

The Company's purpose here omits the purchase and sale of Portfolio Loans and co-investment, co-ownership and co-lending, which Note Purchase Agreement §3.7 expressly includes in the same purpose clause. Whether those activities are within the Company's stated purpose depends on which text governs.

'The Company may admit additional or substitute managers' sits against Restricted Actions (c126) and Note Purchase Agreement §6.2(e), which forbid withdrawal of the sole manager without the approval of a Majority in Interest of Noteholders. Whether a substitution of the Manager requires Noteholder consent is unresolved.

The Servicer may be 'one or more qualified servicing entities,' with no definition of what makes a servicing entity qualified and no limit on how many may be engaged. The word 'qualified' carries no ascertainable content here.

'A minimum investment is 20,000 Units, in the discretion of the Manager' does not say whether the minimum itself is subject to the Manager's discretion or only the acceptance of a subscription meeting it. Note Purchase Agreement §1.1 states the point differently, as a 20,000 Unit minimum 'except as may be permitted in the sole discretion of the Company.'

Noteholders are limited to persons who 'qualify as accredited investors' within the meaning of the Securities Act, whereas Note Purchase Agreement §4.1(d) permits a Purchaser who cannot make that representation to purchase if he is sophisticated within Rule 506(b)(2)(ii). Whether a non-accredited but sophisticated investor may hold a Note turns on which document controls.

The defined term '(the "Maturity Date")' is placed at the end of a clause describing the six-month extension, so it is unclear whether the Maturity Date is December 31, 2014, the extended date, or the extension period itself; the same term is then defined again in c092 as the last day of the Note's term. The date on which the Notes fall due is left to construction.

The extension is described as being in the Manager's unfettered discretion, while Note Purchase Agreement §1.6 permits extension only for orderly liquidation of Portfolio Loans and only on ninety days' prior written notice to Noteholders. Whether those conditions bind the extension must be resolved.

The Floating Rate 'will not be less than 8% on an annualized basis for a calendar year,' whereas the Executive Summary (c016) promises 'a minimum average rate of eight percent (8%) annualized.' An annual floor and an average minimum produce different entitlements where quarterly rates vary.

Roll-over is available only if 'the Noteholder is a qualified investor at the time of the making of the request,' a term used repeatedly (c096, c098) but never defined in the Memorandum, which elsewhere speaks of 'accredited investors' (c087, c209). Who is a qualified investor cannot be determined from the instrument.

This bullet defines '(the "Maturity Date")' as the last day of the Note's term, but the same term was already defined in the term bullet (c088) in connection with the six-month extension. The instrument carries two definitions of the same operative date.

The pro rata payment rule for periods of insufficient funds cannot be squared with the Company's discretionary power to prepay individual Notes (c103) and with Note Purchase Agreement §1.4(b), which permits prepayment of selected ERISA and regulatory-driven Noteholders ahead of others. Whether ratable treatment or selective prepayment governs would have to be decided.

Repayment is stated to be secured by an interest in the assets of the Company without qualification, while Company Borrowings (c125) and Note Purchase Agreement §2.3(b) make that Lien subordinate to the liens of any Company Borrowing. The quality of the security promised here depends on provisions elsewhere.

This provision has the Company issue a Note 'in the principal amount of such purchase,' but the additional-Unit provisions (c096, c098) say the Note will not be reissued and only Company records will show the increase, so the instrument's face amount ceases to state the Principal. What evidences a Noteholder's Principal is left to be construed.

Increases in Units are effective on a closing and reflected only in Company records, which cannot be squared with the Payment for Notes term (c095) under which the Note is issued in the principal amount of the purchase. A Noteholder's Principal and his Note's stated amount would diverge.

The Company is entitled to retain 'any interest earned' on subscription funds in the Closing Account, whereas Note Purchase Agreement §2.2(b) allows a Purchaser to retain any interest or fees paid directly to him for the same pre-qualification period. Entitlement to earnings on subscription money is stated differently in the two documents.

The Pre-Investment Account is described as 'a segregated account owned by the Company' held with an unaffiliated institutional lender, while Note Purchase Agreement §2.4(a) describes a Company bank account 'for the purpose of receiving and pooling funds from Noteholders.' Whether Noteholder funds are segregated or pooled before investment is stated inconsistently.

Funds remaining after payment of the purchase price 'shall be returned by the Company' with no time fixed, whereas Note Purchase Agreement §2.2(d) requires return within five business days after the closing. When the obligation to return matures cannot be determined from this provision.

The provision permits withdrawal 'at any time until his subscription has been accepted' and requires prompt return, while Note Purchase Agreement §2.2(d) requires written notice as provided in the subscription agreement and return, without interest, within five business days. The mechanics of withdrawal differ between the documents.

The prepayment conditions stated here omit the further condition in Note Purchase Agreement §1.4(a)(ii)(C) that the Company determine the prepayment will not adversely affect its obligations or liquidity, and the §1.4(b) power to prepay ERISA Noteholders before the Minimum Holding Period. The conditions governing a prepayment request are not the same in the two documents.

Here 'the Company will appoint' the Collateral Agent and grant it powers in addition to those in the Noteholder Agreements, whereas Note Purchase Agreement §9(a) provides that 'the Manager will appoint a non-Affiliated collateral agent' whose powers are those granted in the Security Agreement. Who appoints and empowers the Noteholders' representative differs between the documents.

Acceleration on bankruptcy or dissolution is excepted 'to the extent the Company's obligations ... have been assumed by an affiliate of or successor in interest to the Company,' without defining what assumption suffices, who may effect it, or whether Noteholder consent is needed. The carve-out could swallow the acceleration right entirely.

This summary term states an acceleration right that has no counterpart in the Note Purchase Agreement, which contains no acceleration or event-of-default provision at all, and the Memorandum elsewhere says the Summary is qualified in its entirety by that agreement (c080, c215). Whether Noteholders have any acceleration right on the Company's bankruptcy therefore has to be construed across the documents.

Additional members may be admitted 'in [the Manager's] discretion and with the requisite approval of members,' but neither the Memorandum nor this provision states what approval is requisite, and the Manager is the sole initial member. The condition is incapable of application as drafted.

The final closing is fixed at the last day of the sixth full quarter after the Initial Closing (estimated June 30, 2009), while the Executive Summary (c015) says closings are expected monthly 'through May 1, 2009' and Note Purchase Agreement §2.1 measures the Subscription Period from the fiscal quarter of the Initial Closing. The date after which no Notes may be sold differs across the three statements.

The Manager is said to bear 'the operating, legal and administrative expenses of the Company,' whereas Note Purchase Agreement §5.5(a) provides that the Company shall bear all costs, fees and expenses of its formation, operation and general administration, including legal and accounting fees. Who pays the Company's operating and legal costs is stated in opposite terms in the two documents.

This term caps Company Expenses at the greater of $500,000 or 1% of outstanding Principal, whereas Note Purchase Agreement §5.5(a) makes the Company bear all costs of formation, operation and administration with no cap at all. Whether the Company's expense burden is capped depends on which document governs.

The cap phrase 'not to exceed a maximum of $500,000 or 1% of aggregate Principal of outstanding Notes, whichever amount is greater' is placed after 'organizational fees and costs' but before the listed taxes, accounting, audit, communications and rent, so it is unclear whether the ceiling covers the whole list or only organizational costs. The syntax leaves the scope of the cap undetermined.

The reimbursement obligation is unlimited, which cannot be squared with the dollar ceiling on Company Expenses in the immediately preceding term (c112). A cap on the Company's expenses and an uncapped duty to reimburse the Manager for those same expenses cannot both operate.

The Loan Service Fee is payable by the Company 'to the Servicer,' whereas Note Purchase Agreement §5.4 provides that the Company shall pay the Loan Servicing Fee to the Manager (or the Manager's designee). Who is the Company's payee for servicing compensation differs between the documents.

Processing and documentation fees are put at 'approximately $1,000 - $2,000 per Portfolio Loan' here, while the Compensation to Management table in Section III states they are 'anticipated to average approximately $1,000 per loan.' The two statements of the same charge to Portfolio Borrowers do not agree.

This provision routes borrower-paid fees and commissions to the Servicer, and to the Manager only where the Manager contracts directly with the Servicer, whereas Note Purchase Agreement §5.4(c)-(f) entitles the Manager to those amounts in all events. The entitlement to Commissions, Loan Fees and Documentation Fees is allocated differently by the two documents.

Loan Service Expenses are placed on the Servicer alone, while Note Purchase Agreement §5.5(a) says such expenses 'shall be borne by the Manager or the Servicer.' Which affiliate must absorb them if the Servicer does not is left unresolved.

The permission to take fees and equity interests in Portfolio Borrowers is made 'subject to restrictions with respect to Affiliated Transactions,' a capitalized term nowhere defined in the Memorandum. The only content for it lies in Note Purchase Agreement §5.7, to which this provision does not refer.

The sentence says the Company will be restricted 'in the amount of compensation it may receive,' but the Company pays rather than receives the compensation described throughout Section V (c110, c114, c119). The word 'receive' inverts the restriction it purports to summarise.

'The Company's initial term will terminate at the Manager's election upon the first to occur of (i) ... or (ii)' does not say whether termination is automatic on the earlier event or requires an election the Manager may withhold indefinitely. The life of the Company, and hence of the Collateral, turns on that ambiguity.

Transfers are permitted without consent 'for certain transfers to family trusts, to wholly-owned affiliates or by operation of law,' whereas Note Purchase Agreement §7 makes the Notes non-negotiable and forbids any assignment or transfer without the Company's consent, which may be withheld in its sole and absolute discretion, declaring any attempted transfer null and void. The two provisions cannot both be given effect on a transfer to a family trust.

A Company Borrowing is defined here as a borrowing 'from an unaffiliated lender,' while Note Purchase Agreement §5.3(a) lets the Manager incur Company Borrowings on any terms it determines and §5.7(f) permits the Manager, Members and Affiliates to lend to the Company. Whether affiliate lending can obtain the priority described here must be construed.

The consent requirement applies to the five listed actions 'among other restrictions,' a catch-all that leaves it unclear whether any action beyond the enumerated ones requires a Majority in Interest's approval. The specific list and the open-ended phrase pull against each other.

The Manager is to devote such business time 'as may be necessary to perform its obligations,' while the Allocation of Management Time discussion (c051) says the Manager and Principals will devote 'only so much time ... as is reasonably required' and Note Purchase Agreement §6.1(c) fixes the standard as reasonably necessary to manage the Company effectively. Three different formulations of the same commitment appear.

Reports beyond tax information are left to whatever 'the Manager, in its discretion, may determine,' whereas Note Purchase Agreement §6.1(d) obliges the Company to keep books audited annually by an independent accountant and open to Noteholder inspection on reasonable notice. The Noteholders' information rights are materially different under the two documents.

The flat statement that Noteholders 'will not be allocated any tax items' cannot be squared with the recharacterization discussion (c142, c151), which contemplates that Noteholders may be treated as members receiving allocable Company income. Whether this term is a promise or an intention is left open.

The sentence is ungrammatical and self-contradictory: 'The Company Agreement may not be amended without the approval of a Majority in Interest of Noteholders (i) violates the Company's obligations ... or (ii) modifies the general purpose of the Company' omits the conditional ('if the amendment'), so as written it forbids all amendments without consent. The consent trigger cannot be read off the words used.

Even repaired, this consent trigger — amendments that violate the Investor Documents or modify the Company's general purpose — differs from Note Purchase Agreement §6.3, which requires Majority in Interest approval for amendments that materially and adversely affect the Noteholders' economic interests. The class of amendments needing consent differs between the documents.

The first sentence makes every modification or waiver of a Noteholder Agreement subject to approval by the Company and a Majority in Interest, while the second lets any individual Noteholder waive or modify any provision as to his own Note with only the Manager's consent. The two sentences give inconsistent answers on who may alter a Note's terms.

Indemnification is denied only for 'willful misconduct or gross negligence,' whereas the earlier description of the same indemnity (c036) states the exclusion as 'fraud, bad faith or willful misconduct.' Conduct that is grossly negligent, or in bad faith, is covered under one formulation and excluded under the other.

The power of attorney granted by Noteholders is described as covering 'documents that the Members have expressly agreed to execute,' but Noteholders are expressly not Members (c107, c018) and Note Purchase Agreement §8.1 grants the power for the Noteholders' own documents. The class of documents the Manager may sign in a Noteholder's name is misdescribed.

The summary is stated to apply only to U.S. Holders who hold the Notes as 'capital assets,' yet the Gain or Loss discussion (c148) says any gain on disposition of a Note will generally be ordinary income because the Notes are contingent debt instruments. Whose tax position the summary actually describes is left unclear.

This paragraph contemplates that Note ownership may be recharacterized as equity ownership in the Company, which cannot be squared with the flat statements that Noteholders will not own any equity interest and will be allocated no tax items (c018, c129). The recharacterization discussion undercuts the terms it is supposed to describe.

The Notes are to be treated as 'contingent debt instruments' paying 'additional interest,' although the Note terms (c089, c092) provide only for a floating rate with an 8% floor and no contingent payment is described anywhere in the Memorandum. What the contingent element of the Notes is cannot be identified from the instrument.

The paragraph defines and uses 'Comparable Yield' and then refers to a 'higher or lower Comparative Yield,' a term that appears nowhere else. The substitution leaves it uncertain whether a different measure is meant.

The disclaimer that the 8% Comparable Yield 'does not constitute a projection or representation as to the amounts that Noteholders will actually receive' sits against the Executive Summary's 8% target (c012) and the 8% rate floor (c089). Whether 8% is a representation or merely a tax computation is left to construction.

The parenthetical defines 'unrelated business taxable income' as '(UBT)', but every later use in the same discussion (c150, c151) is 'UBTI'. The defined abbreviation and the term actually used do not match.

The paragraph states that if Noteholders were characterized as members 'amounts received with respect to the Notes would not be treated as UBTI,' and then immediately says income from Portfolio Loans funded by Company Borrowings and from foreclosed property would generate UBTI to such investors. The same recharacterization is said both to produce and not to produce UBTI.

Plan Investors 'must not rely upon the Manager or its affiliates for investment advice,' whereas the Conflicts of Interest sections tell Noteholders they 'must rely on the good faith and integrity of the Manager and Servicer' (c038, c040, c050). The two instructions on reliance point in opposite directions for the same investor.

The provision says the operation will be structured 'so as not to subject the Fund' to the Investment Company Act and then, 'in the alternative,' that the Company expects to rely on the section 3(c)(5) exemption — two inconsistent positions, and 'the Fund' is not the defined entity ('the Company'). What the Company has actually undertaken about registration cannot be determined.

This section says only that the Company 'may be deemed a borrower and the Noteholders may be deemed lenders,' while the Executive Summary describes investors as 'loaning' their capital to the Company (c015) and as secured creditors (c018), and the Note Purchase Agreement §1.1 makes each Purchaser agree 'to lend to the Company.' Whether the relationship is a loan or a securities purchase is characterized inconsistently.

The Usury discussion admits that the rates payable to Noteholders 'may exceed the applicable statutorily-defined usury rates,' which cannot be squared with the Company's unqualified obligation to pay a Floating Rate of no less than 8% (c089) and the guaranteed minimum return described in the Executive Summary (c016). Whether the promised rate is enforceable is thrown into doubt by this provision.

The Company's compliance undertaking is limited to reliance on advisors and 'commercially reasonable efforts,' a standard the Memorandum never defines and against which no benchmark is given. The extent of the Company's usury-compliance obligation cannot be measured.

This provision treats each Noteholder as a lender who may need a finance lender's licence in his own jurisdiction, whereas the offering is elsewhere described as a private placement of securities to accredited investors (c087, c160) who are merely passive purchasers (c203). Whether Noteholders bear licensing obligations turns on which characterization controls.

This provision says the Company expects to make its Portfolio Loans 'pursuant to a finance lender's license issued by California,' while the Memorandum elsewhere identifies only Bar-K, Inc. and R.E. Loans as licensed California finance lenders (c030, c047) and has the Servicer originating all loans (c031). Whose licence the lending is conducted under is not consistently stated.

The lender-liability discussion warns that a court could subject the Noteholders' debt to equitable subordination and deny them 'the preferred status of a creditor in a bankruptcy,' which cannot be squared with the unqualified statement that Noteholders will be secured creditors (c018) and with the Acceleration term (c106). The Noteholders' priority is described in two incompatible ways.

The Risk Factors open by stating that the purchase of Notes 'will involve a high degree of risk,' whereas the Executive Summary offers 'superior returns with a conservative risk profile' (c012). A court would have to decide which characterization the investor was entitled to rely on.

'Typically a Portfolio Borrower will be structured as a single purpose entity or venture' is difficult to square with the lending criteria, which contemplate loans to individuals and to borrowers consolidating their debts (c056, c063). Who the Company's borrowers will be is described inconsistently.

The closing sentence refers to 'the inability of the Portfolio Manager to repay such Loan,' but no 'Portfolio Manager' is defined anywhere in the Memorandum; the obligor is the Portfolio Borrower. The sentence names a party that does not exist in the instrument.

The risk factor states that 'the Project Owner will not have the capacity to repay all or a portion of the Portfolio Loans,' but 'Project Owner' is not a defined term in the Memorandum, which speaks of the Portfolio Borrower. Whose incapacity is described is left uncertain.

The Company is said to be limited 'by law or by the terms of its loan agreement,' without identifying which agreement is meant — the Note Purchase Agreement, the Security Agreement, or a Company Borrowing. The source of the limitation cannot be identified from the words used.

'Portfolio Loans will generally not be personal obligations of the applicable borrowers' sits against Credit Evaluations (c063), which has the Manager considering the creditworthiness of the borrower 'and any guarantor' in deciding ability to repay. Whether recourse to borrowers or guarantors exists is stated two ways.

'A Project will be released as collateral as it is sold and the payment is made on the Portfolio Loan' does not state what payment is required for release or who fixes it, in a provision that otherwise governs cross-collateralized loans. The release condition has no ascertainable content.

This risk factor says only that the Company 'intends to require' Portfolio Borrowers to maintain adequate insurance, whereas the Escrow Conditions (c066) make satisfactory fire and casualty insurance naming the Company as loss payee a mandatory condition of any disbursement. An intention and a funding condition are made to do the same work.

The provision contemplates that the Company may fund the purchase of senior notes 'through capital raised from Noteholders or new investors,' although no subscriptions for Units may be accepted after the final closing (c096, c109). The assumed funding source may be unavailable for most of the Notes' term.

Compliance with lending laws is entrusted to 'commercially reasonable efforts in reliance on qualified advisors, including its affiliate Bar-K, Inc.', with no definition of what makes an advisor qualified and with the affiliate Servicer cast as the compliance advisor. Neither the standard of effort nor the qualification of the advisor can be measured.

This risk factor says the structure of the Portfolio Loans 'is expected to comply with California usury laws,' while the Usury discussion in Section VI (c163) states that the rates payable by Portfolio Borrowers 'may exceed the applicable statutorily-defined usury rates.' The two passages give different accounts of the Company's usury exposure.

The Manager and its members are said to 'receive Company gains and certain other income' disproportionate to their capital, whereas the compensation terms (c110, c114, c121) describe the Manager's entitlement as fees and third-party payments only, and all tax items are allocated to Members (c129). What the Manager actually takes out of the Company is described inconsistently.

Investors are told they must entrust 'valuation of the Projects' entirely to the Manager, whereas the Loan-to-Value Ratios provision (c060) and the affiliate-sale pricing standards (c054) contemplate independent written appraisals. Whether any independent valuation constrains the Manager must be construed.

This heading and paragraph subject the purchase of Notes to 'risks that are typical of investments in private equity funds,' although the Notes are debt and Noteholders are expressly not equity holders (c018, c140). Whether the investment is being characterized as equity or debt is left unresolved.

The warning that the portfolio 'may become concentrated in a limited number of portfolio loans' sits against Loan Diversification (c075), which forbids any new loan commitment exceeding 20% of Company capital after the second year. Whether the diversification limit binds or merely describes an aspiration must be construed.

This risk factor states there is 'no assurance that the Noteholders' security interest will be perfected in seniority over the interests of other creditors' or that its remedies will be enforceable, which cannot be squared with the Executive Summary's statement that the Notes will be secured by the assets of the Company and that Noteholders are secured creditors (c012, c018). What security the Noteholders bargained for turns on which passage governs.

Transferability is said to be 'severely restricted by the Note Purchase Agreement, the terms of the Note and by federal and state securities laws,' whereas the Transfers of Notes term (c124) permits transfers to family trusts, wholly-owned affiliates and by operation of law without consent. The extent of the restriction is stated differently in the two provisions.

The statement that the structure 'precludes the Noteholders from ... voting on Company operating matters' cannot be squared with Restricted Actions (c126), Amendment of Company Agreement (c130) and Amendments, Waivers (c131), each of which requires the approval of a Majority in Interest of Noteholders. Noteholders are said both to have and not to have voting rights over Company matters.

This risk factor defines the Investment Company Act of 1940 as 'the Company Act,' a label that collides with the Memorandum's other defined terms — the 'Investment Company Act' (c003, c159) and the 'Company Agreement' (c080). The same statute is given two different defined names within one instrument.

The concluding paragraph again invokes the Principals' 'favorable track record with making loans similar to those targeted for the Company,' which the historical-results disclaimer (c026) says may not be relied on as any indication of the Company's results. Whether the track record is a representation or disclaimed illustration remains unresolved.

Every investor is required to represent that he is an 'Accredited Investor' within Rule 501, whereas Note Purchase Agreement §4.1(d) expressly permits a Purchaser who cannot make that representation to buy Notes if he is sophisticated within Rule 506(b)(2)(ii). The eligibility condition for purchasing a Note differs between the two documents.

Paragraph 2 admits an entity 'formed for the purpose of purchasing a Note' provided each beneficial owner qualifies, while paragraph 1(v) (c209) admits a corporation, partnership, LLC or business trust only if it is 'not formed for the purpose of acquiring the Note.' The two paragraphs give opposite answers for the same purpose-formed entity.

The investor must represent that he acquires the Note 'not directly or indirectly for the account of any other person whatsoever,' yet the accredited-investor criteria admit trusts and entities purchasing for their beneficial owners (c209(ii), (vi)) and the Transfers term allows transfers to family trusts (c124). Whether such holders can truthfully make this representation is left in doubt.

The Company promises to answer questions and provide additional information 'necessary to verify the accuracy of the information furnished,' while the front legend (c009) says no person is authorized to give any information or make any representation other than as contained in the Memorandum. Whether answers given under this section may be relied on must be construed.

This provision makes the Summary of Principal Terms 'qualified in its entirety by reference to the Note Purchase Agreement,' although the Memorandum states terms the Note Purchase Agreement contradicts — transfer exceptions (c124 vs §7) and the allocation of operating expenses (c111 vs §5.5(a)). Whether the Memorandum's terms are displaced wholesale by that agreement is squarely presented.

The sentence describes 'the Company and its Managing Member,' a term the Memorandum never defines and which is inconsistent with the defined 'Manager' and 'Members' (c083, c107). Who is being referred to cannot be determined from the instrument.
